title: Greening power
hookLine: the abbess Hildegard of Bingen spoke of viriditas, the greening life in all things
tomorrow: why is the devil the only one in Hildegard's play who can't sing?

lines: A LEAF THE COLOR OF A LIME.
A LIGHT NO ONE ELSE SAW.
cards: A houseplant stuck in a dark hallway goes pale and leggy. Move it to the window and, a week later, a new leaf unrolls the color of a lime.

The medieval abbess Hildegard of Bingen had a word for that green, and she meant far more than leaves. She lived in the Rhineland, and since she was a girl she had been seeing a light no one else saw.
She kept it mostly to herself. Then, in her own telling, a voice came out of the light: write what you see and hear. She refused.
She was afraid of what people would say. And she fell sick, flat in her bed, until she picked up the pen.

teach.b: She wrote, and the book became Scivias, a book of her visions. Running through her writing and her songs is one Latin word: viriditas, greenness. For Hildegard it isn't only the color of leaves.

teach.h: GOD'S LIFE SHOWING UP IN THE WORLD.
teach.b: It's God's own life showing up in the world: the sap rising in a tree, the freshness in a healthy body, the eagerness in a soul that's awake.

teach.h: THE OPPOSITE: A SOUL GONE DRY.
teach.b: Its opposite, in her writing, is dryness, a soul gone brittle and fruitless. In one of her songs she greets Mary as the greenest branch: O viridissima virga, ave.

teach.h: THE GREEN COMES BACK FROM INSIDE.
teach.b: Here is the teaching under it, from Hildegard's Benedictine Christian faith. God's life isn't locked away in heaven.

It greens in creation and in people, so caring for bodies, gardens and souls is part of holiness, not a distraction from it. That's why this abbess also wrote about plants and healing. And look at her own story again.
The woman who hid what she'd been given went dry and sick.
When she let it out into words, she got up. In her picture a dry season isn't proof that God has left. The green comes back from inside, the way sap returns to a branch that looked dead all winter.

how: Hildegard's songs are sung by choirs and by monastic communities, and Catholics honor her as a saint and a Doctor of the Church; readers still study her visions in Scivias and her writings on plants and healing.

o: the bright light Hildegard saw in her visions
a greening life that shows God in growing things
a Latin word for a garden kept inside a monastery

p: greenness: God's life in the world
a soul gone brittle and fruitless
what she called Mary in a song
the book she wrote after refusing

s: for Hildegard, viriditas meant only the color of plants
it was God's life showing up everywhere: in trees, in healthy bodies, in an awake soul.
Hildegard wrote down her visions the moment she was told to
in her own telling she refused, out of fear of what people would say, and fell sick until she wrote.
Hildegard wrote about plants and healing as well as visions
caring for bodies and growing things was part of holiness for her, not a distraction from it.

games.q: a friend who used to love her church choir says she feels nothing when she sings now, so it must be over. what fits Hildegard's greening?
o: a dry stretch isn't proof the life is gone; in Hildegard's picture the green returns from inside.
feeling nothing means it was never real, so she should stop for good.
she should force herself to feel joy every time, or she's doing it wrong.
games.why: Hildegard set greenness against dryness, and in her own story the dry, sick stretch ended when she wrote.

practice: Find one green and growing thing: a plant on the sill, a weed in a crack, a tree outside the window. Look at it closely for two minutes, the veins, the new edges, the places still unfolding.
Let Hildegard's word sit with you while you look: greening.

wordCard.voice: Viriditas: Hildegard's Latin word for greenness, God's life showing up in plants, bodies and souls.

orig.note: Latin: greenness. Hildegard, a Benedictine abbess, used it for God's life in creation.

carryVoice: Your line: greening. Dry is a season, and in Hildegard's picture the green comes back from inside. Day 1583, done.
